standard.title: Experiment to develop skills
standard.description: experiment with visual conventions, visual arts processes and materials to develop skills
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can use visual conventions, processes and materials with increasing control (AC9AVA6D01). They have not yet systematically experimented to develop skills through deliberate practice, nor documented and evaluated that process using visual arts terminology.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students experiment with visual conventions, processes and materials to develop skills, documenting and evaluating their practice using visual arts terminology.

nodes.label: Purposeful experimentation with materials and processes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can experiment with a visual convention, process or material with a clear purpose — to discover what it can do — and document what the experimentation reveals
nodes.minimum_width: Experiment with at least one visual convention, process or material; document at least two outcomes and describe what each reveals about what the material or process can do
nodes.typical_width: Experiment with a range of materials, processes or conventions across the unit; approach each experiment with a question or purpose; document outcomes using visual arts terminology
wider: Investigate how artists use encryption, layering or symbolic content and experiment with these approaches — document what the technique adds to meaning-making in own work
Experiment with sustainable materials (natural dyes, recycled materials) and document how material constraints generate rather than limit creative possibilities
Study how a specific artist uses a particular material or process and experiment with replicating and then diverging from that approach — document what is learned through the divergence

response_modes.reason: Purposeful experimentation — setting a question, trying approaches, documenting outcomes using correct terminology — is a studio practice habit that develops through repeated cycles, not through exposure to more material types. The skill is in the discipline of the process itself: students need to practise the documentation cycle until it becomes habitual.

success_criteria: Experiments with at least one convention, process or material with a clear purpose
Documents at least two outcomes using visual arts terminology
Describes what the experimentation reveals — not just what was tried

nodes.label: Learning from other artists to inform own experimentation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate how other artists use materials and processes and use these insights to direct their own experimentation
nodes.minimum_width: Investigate how at least one artist uses a specific material or process; use this as a starting point for own experimentation; document the connection
nodes.typical_width: Investigate multiple artists' approaches to materials and processes; use the investigation to set specific experimentation goals; document how the investigation informed the direction of own experimentation
wider: Explore how artists respond to sensory qualities of materials as inspiration — experiment with allowing material properties to direct the work rather than imposing a plan
Compare how artists working in different cultural traditions respond to the same material — use the comparison to develop own informed approach
Investigate how an artist's choice of material carries meaning beyond technical function — experiment with making material choice a deliberate expressive decision in own work

response_modes.reason: Students commonly look at other artists' work and describe what they see without reasoning through how it informs their own decisions — the investigation stays at appreciation rather than becoming analytical. Scaffolding the connection (what specific technique or choice am I investigating, what does it do, how would I try it, what would I change?) builds the transfer from investigation to practice.

success_criteria: Investigates at least one artist's use of a material or process
Uses the investigation to set a specific experimentation direction — not just 'I was inspired'
Documents the connection between the investigation and own experimentation outcomes

nodes.label: Evaluating experimentation with feedback
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate their own experimentation using teacher and peer feedback, and use evaluation to set future practice directions
nodes.minimum_width: Respond to at least one piece of teacher or peer feedback on own experimentation; document how the feedback changes subsequent practice direction
nodes.typical_width: Use teacher and peer feedback to evaluate own experimentation outcomes; set future goals based on evaluation; document the feedback-evaluation-decision cycle using visual arts terminology
wider: Develop a systematic evaluation process for own studio practice — use Viewpoints to generate questions that push reflection beyond surface assessment
Evaluate own experimentation against the work of artists investigated — identify specific points of comparison and what they reveal about own skill development
Develop criteria for evaluating own experimentation that go beyond 'it worked/didn't work' — use visual arts vocabulary to articulate what success looks like at multiple levels

response_modes.reason: Using feedback productively — receiving it, interpreting it in relation to visual arts criteria, and translating it into changed practice — is a reflective habit that develops through repeated cycles. Students need sustained practice with the feedback loop rather than exposure to more experimentation contexts.

success_criteria: Responds to at least one piece of feedback with a documented change in practice direction
Evaluation uses visual arts terminology — not just 'I liked it' or 'it didn't work'
